title: HTTP Methods, Headers, Status Codes, TCP Framing & HTTP vs. HTTPS/TLS
topic: HTTP Requests/Responses, Methods, Headers, Status Codes, HTTP vs. HTTPS, TLS Basics
learning_objectives: Observe an actual HTTP/1.1 request/response exchange running atop a real TCP three-way handshake.
Inspect HTTP methods (GET, POST), request/response headers, and status codes (200 OK vs. 404 Not Found).
Explain why ordinary packet capture shows plaintext HTTP headers but CANNOT read encrypted HTTPS (TLS) application payloads.

concept_explanation.title: HTTP/1.1 Layered Over TCP
concept_explanation.summary: HTTP is an application-layer request-response protocol built on top of TCP. Before a single HTTP byte is sent, TCP completes its 3-way handshake.
key_points: Requests carry a request line (METHOD path HTTP/1.1), headers (Host, User-Agent, Content-Length), and optional body.
Responses return a status line (e.g., 200 OK, 404 Not Found, 500 Internal Server Error), headers, and body.

concept_explanation.title: HTTP vs. HTTPS & TLS Encryption Boundary
concept_explanation.summary: HTTPS inserts TLS between TCP and HTTP. After the TCP handshake, client and server complete a TLS handshake to verify server identity (certificates) and negotiate symmetric session keys.
key_points: Under HTTPS, packet capture still sees IP addresses, TCP ports (443), TCP flags, and TLS handshake metadata (e.g., SNI), NOT decrypted HTTP URLs, headers, or bodies.
Never pretend an ordinary packet capture can inspect encrypted HTTPS application payloads without session keys.

experiment.title: Start an Ephemeral Local HTTP Server & Capture Real GET/POST/404 Exchanges
experiment.instructions: Launches a safe ephemeral Python HTTP/1.1 server bound strictly to 127.0.0.1, executes real HTTP requests, captures the underlying TCP packets with libpcap, and records exact HTTP status codes and headers.
required_setup: Phase 4 libpcap capture helper for real TCP packet capture
execution_steps: Run 'HTTP GET 200 OK & POST Echo' and inspect the captured TCP 3-way handshake, data transfer, and real HTTP headers.
Run 'HTTP 404 Not Found' to compare transport success (TCP completed cleanly!) with application-layer 404 status.
Switch to the Packets tab and verify how HTTP rides inside TCP PSH+ACK segments.

supported_scenarios.label: 1. Local HTTP GET (200 OK) & POST Echo
supported_scenarios.description: Starts ephemeral localhost HTTP server, performs GET / and POST /echo, captures real TCP packets and headers.

supported_scenarios.label: 2. Failed HTTP Resource Request (404 Not Found)
supported_scenarios.description: Requests a missing route (/does-not-exist) to distinguish TCP connection success from HTTP 404 error.

expected_observations: TCP handshake (SYN -> SYN+ACK -> ACK) completes BEFORE the HTTP GET request is transmitted.
HTTP 404 still has a successful TCP 3-way handshake and graceful FIN teardown — 404 is an Application Layer status.
Real HTTP status codes and headers (Content-Type, Content-Length, Server) are captured from the live exchange.
observation_caveats: Packet capture remains header-only by default for privacy; observed HTTP status/headers come from the controlled lab client.
With HTTPS/TLS, wire packet capture sees encrypted ciphertext records, never plaintext HTTP headers or bodies.

questions.prompt: A client requests GET /missing from a running HTTP server and receives '404 Not Found'. What does the TCP layer show?
options: TCP connect() fails with ECONNREFUSED and sends RST.
TCP completes a normal 3-way handshake, delivers the HTTP request and 404 response reliably, and closes normally.
TCP retransmits the GET request 404 times.
No TCP packets are generated for 404 errors.
questions.rubric_summary: 404 is an HTTP (L7) status delivered over a completely healthy TCP (L4) connection.
questions.explanation: TCP only guarantees reliable delivery between sockets. Because the server accepted the connection and sent an HTTP 404 payload, the TCP handshake and delivery both succeeded.

questions.prompt: When capturing packets of an HTTPS (TLS) connection with ordinary libpcap (without TLS session keys), which of the following can you legitimately observe?
options: The plaintext HTTP Authorization header and cookies.
The JSON body returned by the API.
IP addresses, TCP ports/flags/sequence numbers, packet sizes, and timing — but NOT the decrypted HTTP payload.
questions.rubric_summary: IP/TCP headers and sizes remain visible; HTTP headers and body are encrypted by TLS.
questions.explanation: TLS encrypts Layer 7 HTTP content, leaving Layer 3/4 headers (IP, TCP ports, flags, packet lengths, timing) observable on the wire.

questions.prompt: Explain the difference between an idempotent HTTP GET request and a POST request, and name one header commonly included in a POST.
questions.rubric_summary: GET retrieves a resource without side effects; POST submits data in the body with Content-Length / Content-Type.
questions.explanation: GET retrieves representations safely/idempotently without a request body, whereas POST submits payload data (described by Content-Type and Content-Length headers) to create or process state.
